title: Level up your back
summary: Third in the Level Up series: NH argues the upper back is the most underrated and underdeveloped muscle group in naturals and explains how to fix it. He wants high-frequency training split across the week instead of a back day, the lower back treated as a stabilizing bridge, mostly legless pulls so the lower back doesn't limit volume, and back work used as Lego blocks and supersets to fill any program.
claims: The upper back is the most underdeveloped muscle group in natural lifters because it is underrated; many natural physiques are overdeveloped in front versus back
Naturals have no special limit on upper back size; an underdeveloped back is always due to training practices
NH trained for years with an upper back that stayed flat with no ridges or 3D pop because he only hit it as an assistant to prime movers
The upper back is many muscles that can be targeted separately; no exercise hits it all equally, so a one-compound-hits-all approach fails
Deadlifts work the lats only a little; you will never have developed lats from deadlifts alone
A muscle that only assists a compound rarely grows; e.g. most people won't grow big biceps from chin-ups alone; prioritize each muscle you want to grow
The opposite extreme, trying to hit every tiny fiber and memorizing anatomy, causes over-specialization and doesn't improve training
For practical purposes the upper back is everything behind you between the base of the neck and the hips: lower back, erectors, lats, rhomboids, teres, traps and rear delts
True isolation is a myth since muscles work together, but movements do prioritize some muscles and deprioritize others, which is what makes programming possible
A lift that hit every muscle equally would be the worst lift because it couldn't be programmed or matched to recovery
Most viewers are novices to intermediates and don't need surgical precision: just hit the back and stop doing so many rows
Never have a day where you only train the back; a back day forces pre-fatigue, leaves about 20% of the back getting relevant work, and takes forever
Train the upper back through frequency via separation: spread its parts across the week like puzzle pieces, e.g. traps one day, lats another
Splitting back volume across the week allows more total volume, higher-quality tonnage and better recovery than one weekly session
NH trains legs every two days and never gets sore; soreness is a sign of unpreparedness, not of growth
The upper back recovers fast because it is made of small muscles, and together they still give good work capacity
The lower back is the limiting factor in upper back training and can be trained indirectly, since most back movements recruit it anyway
Think of the lower back as a rigid, neutral bridge between the legs and upper body, never as a mover
For a healthy lower back, stabilization work in squats, floor pulls and horizontal pulls is enough to grow it with good technique
Unlike the abs, the lower back has little stretch potential due to spinal anatomy, which is why bracing alone suffices for it but not for abs
Hyperextensions, bridges and reverse hypers are valid, but they prioritize glutes and hamstrings with the lower back as stabilizer
Legless pulls (cable rows, seal rows, dumbbell rows, vertical pulls with dangling legs) should be the bread and butter for upper back growth
If all back tonnage goes through the lower back it caps volume; e.g. send ~300 lb through the lower back and ~700 lb via legless moves instead of 1,000 lb all through it
If the lower back taps out at 1,000 lb and the upper back at 3,000 lb, only training back through the lower back wastes 2,000 lb of potential
Five years ago inverted rows and seal rows were niche; today's legless, bodybuilding-style back training will produce bigger backs
Back-and-biceps splits are unjustified; the upper back is synergistic with nothing, and forearms get trained by default
Because it is non-synergistic, upper back work can fill gaps left in synergy-based splits such as chest/shoulders/triceps days
Build your split first, then add back movements at the end as Lego blocks so every day is a back day
On a 6-day split: compounds with legs 1-2 days, legless compounds 3-4 days, back isolation 4-6 days out of six
Within a session order back work as leg-involved compounds first, then legless compounds, then isolation, so skipped sets are only isolation
Back isolation includes small cable rows, one-arm standing rows, lateral raises for rear delts and shrugs
Novices should start with one leg-involved back compound plus 1-2 legless compounds and 1-2 isolations per week, then expand
Minimalism is the first step to be expanded later; don't start with expansion or you burn out, and don't stay minimal or you stagnate
Advanced trainees can handle 1-2 heavy leg-involved compounds plus about two horizontal and 2-3 vertical pulls a week at 3-4 sets each, plus isolation
Superset every push with a pull, e.g. bench press then row; it won't hurt performance
Calves, abs, neck and upper back are the easiest superset fillers; the upper back is the 'vanilla ice cream' of the body
Deadlifts can be supersetted with pull-ups; tough on cardio and grip but doesn't hurt performance
Superset shrugs whenever possible, e.g. after heavy pulls or barbell calf raises, to grow a big yoke
Pullovers transformed his lats; do them 1x/week at first, then medium-heavy 2-3x/week, never to failure, keep 1-2 RIR to protect the shoulders
Tendons (shoulder, biceps tendon, forearm) give out long before the upper back gets overtrained; watch tendon pain from too many pull-ups
Vary pull-up grips (neutral, supinated, pronated, fat grips, towels) to avoid tendon pain
Don't do a horizontal pull on consecutive days; e.g. horizontal Monday, isolation Tuesday, vertical Wednesday, horizontal Thursday
Scale back the frequency numbers for a 3-day schedule; they were given for a 6-day split
Ignore the 'pull twice as much as you push' rule; NH pulls far more than twice what he pushes because pulling is his priority
Train the back whenever there is a window; it's low impact if legs aren't involved
A thick upper back should be the mark of a seasoned lifter, like forearms and legs that fill out with age
exercises: heavy leg-involved back compound; only small lat stimulus
removes lower back as limiting factor
strict, no cheating with legs/lower back
vary grips: neutral, supinated, pronated, fat grips, towels
vertical pull; grip variation prevents tendon pain
rear delt work as back isolation
superset after pulls or calf raises
easy yoke volume that fits anywhere
transformed his lats; protects shoulder joint
valid, but mainly glutes and hamstrings
pair every push with a pull
adds back volume without hurting performance
